pr_title: fips: update DSA security check to fix legacy verify strengths
pr_body:
3.0.x will need a change to the fips version line in the test (to >3.0.10)

Refer SP 800-131Ar2 table 2:
    https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-131a/rev-2/final

Fixes #21185

- [x] tests are added or updated
pr_comments: Looks like you have some test failures..

Test failures should be addressed, not in an ideal way.

I don't seem to be able to generate a key from the command line that can't be use for verification by the FIPS provider (i.e. either L < 512 or N < 160).

> 3.0.x will need a change to the fips version line in the test (to >3.0.10)

That's questionable - Don't you with the fips provider compat tests test 3.0 tip of the branch with for example 3.1.1 (as the validated FIPS module?) -> it would fail that test then.

Otherwise, keeping the FIPSversion check as is IMO just means the legacy key verification won't be tested which is IMO acceptable.
Happy to omit the test on back port, that's reasonable.
Dropping commit 5b81e5f446fe5156f72ea4407bf5cdbdd1c0959e since that restriction has been there forever and doesn't impact the reported issue.
This pull request is ready to merge

issue_context.title: Incorrect DSA verification check in FIPS provider
issue_context.body:
From openssl-users:

> Our organization signs image artifacts with 2048-bit DSA keys before releasing them to the field. Some of these signatures fail to verify when using the OpenSSL 3.0 FIPS provider. It turns out that while most of our signing keys are (L,N)=(2048,256), two early keys created long ago are (2048,160) and the signatures that fail to verify were created with these keys. Disabling security checks in the configuration file resolves this but I'd prefer not do that and inadvertently let something else non-compliant go undetected.
> 
> I discovered this code in providers/common/securitycheck.c:
> 
> ```c
>         /*
>          * For Digital signature verification DSA keys with < 112 bits of
>          * security strength (i.e L < 2048 bits), are still allowed for legacy
>          * use. The bounds given in SP800 131Ar2 - Table 2 are
>          * (512 <= L < 2048 and 160 <= N < 224)
>          */
>         if (!sign && L < 2048)
>             return (L >= 512 && N >= 160 && N < 224);
> ```
> 
> I am by no means an expert in cryptography but this logic does not seem to match my interpretation of the spec which for legacy use allows:
> 
> ```c
>     ((512 <= L < 2048) or (160 <= N < 224))
> ```
> 
> with "or" being the operative word here. OpenSSL is making this an "and" condition. Doesn't 800-131Ar2 allow (2048,160) when verifying a DSA signature, or am I misreading the spec?

review_comments:
I think it would be from a strict reading of the standard which says: `((512 ≤ L < 2048) or (160 ≤ N < 224))`

Satisfying _either_ side makes the _or_ true.  So, 512 ≤ L < 2048 is acceptable regardless of N.  Likewise,160 ≤ N < 224 is acceptable regardless of L.

I think that's stupid so the code is a bit stricter and enforces both lower bounds unconditionally.
Looks like that check has been there since at least 1.1.1

Yeah, that's relevant too.  Fix pushed.

I suspect that the 131Ar2 standard is being silly.  Rather than spelling out legal cases, it just has a blanket statement that's overly broad.

~Does this mean you think we should be checking N = 160, 224 and 256 only despite what 131Ar2 says?~

We shouldn't this breaks backward compatibility.
Maybe OTC decision? I dont mind either way. It has been like this is openSSL for quite some time..

Or just leave the fix with what I did first?  That fixes the original issue just fine.
I doubt anyone is broken by the stricter check in `dsa_do_verify()` given how long it's been there.
yeah probably - I obviously missed it when doing the check..

(L ≥ 512 and N ≥ 160 and (L < 2048 or N < 224))

That's how I read this.  Correct?  It might be good to spell this out in the comment, to make it easier for any reader to compare to the legacy logic in SP 800-131Ar2.

Did you look at 131Ar2? :grin:

There is a comment about this there already.  In what way is it inadequate?
